transcript.content: Hello. What brings you in to see me today?

Hello. Since my divorce, I've been eating huge meals by myself late at night because I’m embarrassed by how much I eat around other people. It's been really hard to deal with on my own, so I finally decided to seek some help.
After these large eating episodes, do you ever try to prevent weight gain by making yourself throw up, using laxatives, fasting, or exercising excessively?

No, I don't do any of those things. I've never forced myself to throw up, used laxatives, or tried to burn it off with extreme exercise. I just end up sitting there on the couch feeling miserable and painfully full.
How many times a week do these late-night eating episodes typically occur, and how many months has this been going on?
This has been happening at least a few nights every week. It's been going on pretty steadily for close to a year now, ever since my divorce was finalized.
During these late-night eating episodes, do you feel a sense of loss of control, as if you can't stop eating or control how much you are consuming?

Yes, completely. Once I start, it's like a switch flips and I just lose all control. I'll be telling myself, "Santiago, stop, this is crazy," but my hands keep going back for more food as if they aren't even listening to me.
During these late-night episodes, do you find yourself eating much faster than normal, or do you eat even when you aren't feeling physically hungry?

Yes, both of those things definitely happen. I eat incredibly fast, barely even chewing, as if I'm in some kind of race to finish. And I frequently eat when I'm not hungry at all, often going back to the kitchen for a second plate or starting on a pan of brownies even when I'm already full.
Apart from the eating episodes, have you been experiencing other symptoms like persistent sadness, constant worry, or difficulty managing your daily responsibilities since the divorce?

Since the divorce, I've been very lonely and my sister has noticed a big change in my mood. It's really affecting my daily life because I'm constantly tired and sluggish at my clerk job from sleeping on a stuffed stomach, and I even skip lunches and turn down weeknight hangouts with my soccer teammates just to "save up" for my eating at night.
After these late-night eating episodes, do you experience intense feelings of guilt, disgust with yourself, or depression about how much you've eaten?

I'm not really sure, to be honest. I definitely feel embarrassed and ashamed, but I haven't really thought about it in terms of intense guilt or depression afterward. I'm usually just focused on how physically uncomfortable and miserable I feel.
How much distress, worry, or emotional pain do these out-of-control eating episodes themselves cause you?

These episodes cause me a great deal of distress, embarrassment, and shame. While it is happening, I feel completely "crazy" and out of control, and afterward, I feel so ashamed of how much I ate that I feel forced to lock myself in my apartment to hide it from my family and friends.
Do you typically wake up from sleep in the middle of the night to eat, or does this late-night eating happen in the evening before you go to sleep?

It happens in the evening before I go to sleep, rather than waking up in the middle of the night. I cook a massive late dinner after getting home from work, eat it all in front of the TV, and then go to bed feeling stuffed and uncomfortable.

The onset of these symptoms, along with low mood and loneliness, was triggered by his divorce one year ago, supporting a comorbid or underlying Adjustment Disorder (F43.2). final_diagnosis.reason: The patient meets the diagnostic criteria for Binge Eating Disorder (classified as F50.8, Other eating disorders, in ICD-10). He describes recurrent episodes of eating large quantities of food late at night with a distinct sense of loss of control. These episodes are characterized by eating much faster than normal, eating when not physically hungry, eating until feeling painfully full, and eating alone due to embarrassment. He experiences marked distress, shame, and embarrassment regarding his eating habits. There is no evidence of regular compensatory behaviors (such as purging, laxative use, or excessive exercise), which rules out Bulimia Nervosa. While his symptoms began after his divorce (suggesting a psychosocial stressor), the clinical presentation is dominated by a fully realized eating disorder, making F50.8 the most specific and appropriate diagnosis over an adjustment disorder (F43.2).
